title: The mobile visit for a fintech product
metaTitle: A fintech product mobile website that decides
excerpt: Most fintech buyers will judge the site on a phone. The first screen still has to show the product, the people responsible, and a way to start.
alt: A pale room with an arched opening onto a dark sofa, a low table, and a glass vase of dried stems, a composed small space for a first screen that has to stay clear on a phone.
caption: A pale room, a dark sofa, a vase of dried stems. The first phone screen should be this composed. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first phone screen of a fintech site?
faqs.answer: The product in a recognizable state, a short line about who is responsible, and a way to open an account or talk to sales. Those three have to fit before the reader scrolls. A headline with no product, or a product with no path, wastes the visit most buyers will actually have.

faqs.question: Should we design the desktop page first?
faqs.answer: Design the phone page first, then let the wider screen add proof and detail. A desktop composition that shrinks until the button falls below a tall image has let the wrong frame decide. If a sentence does not fit on the phone, it does not belong in the opening.

faqs.question: How fast does the mobile page need to be?
faqs.answer: web.dev's Core Web Vitals guidance says a good Largest Contentful Paint is within 2.5 seconds, a good Interaction to Next Paint is 200 milliseconds or less, and a good Cumulative Layout Shift is 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile. On a money page, those targets are how you keep the product and the button from arriving late or jumping.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A fintech product mobile website is the visit most buyers will actually have. The first screen still has to show the product, the people responsible, and a way to start an account or talk to sales.

Do not let the desktop composition decide the phone page. A wide hero that looked balanced on a monitor becomes a tall image, a slogan, and a button the thumb never reaches. Write and design the small screen as the real page.

## The phone is the first draft

Open the design file at a phone width before anyone debates the desktop grid. The constraint is the point. You have a narrow column and a short first view. Into that view you must place a product state, a responsibility line, and one action. If those three do not fit, the page is not ready for a larger canvas. A larger canvas will only add more.

Nielsen Norman Group's research is uncomfortable and useful here. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a page has to make its value clear in about 10 seconds to earn a longer stay. On a phone, those seconds include slow paint, a cookie bar, and a thumb looking for a target. There is no spare strip for a manifesto above the product.

Put the action where the thumb rests, and keep it visible after the first scroll if the page is long. A buyer who has read enough should not have to scroll back through a skyline to find "Open an account." Sticky actions can be right when they are one action and they do not cover the product. Two sticky bars, a chat bubble, and a cookie banner are a crowd. Pick the action.

Type has to be readable without a pinch. If the product screenshot contains the fee or the status, it must still be legible, or the caption must repeat the fact in text. A picture of a UI that becomes a blur on a phone is not proof. It is a texture.

## The first screen, in order

Stack the first screen in the same order as the decision.

1. A short sentence: who it is for and what the product does.
2. The product, cropped to a real state, not a device mock floating in a gradient.
3. One line on who is responsible, or who holds the funds, if that fact is what this buyer checks first.
4. The button: open an account, or talk to sales, with a few words on what happens next.

That stack is the page. Everything else is the rest of the page. Pricing shape can be the next block, still in the column, still in short lines. Proof can follow as one constraint and one decision. Do not insert a logo parade between the product and the button. On a phone, that parade pushes the path off the screen that decides the visit.

Write the sentence so it wraps in two lines, not six. A six-line headline is a paragraph that has not accepted the width. Read it on a device, not in a desktop preview scaled down. The line breaks will be worse than the mock, and the button will sit lower than you think.

If you have two entry paths, stack them only with labels that distinguish them. "Open an account" first if most buyers can self-serve. "Talk to sales" as a text link under it if the other path is real. Two filled buttons of equal weight, one of them saying "Learn more," split the thumb and the decision.

## Trust that still fits in a column

A money buyer will look for accountability even on a small screen. You do not need a certificate badge row. You need the fact, in text, near the product. The entity. The partner bank, if there is one. The thing you do not hold. These lines can be a single sentence under the button. They should not be an image of a badge the screen reader cannot explain and the eye cannot verify.

Save the long security note for a page that can hold it, and link that page with words that say what it is. "Where funds are held" is a link. A lock icon is not. The icon may sit beside the text if the text does the work. Information has to be readable as text, not locked inside a picture. On a phone, pictures are also easy to crop into nonsense. Text survives.

People, if you show them, need a face large enough to be a person and a role in type beside them. A tiny avatar row under a headline does not name anyone. One person, one role, is enough for the first screen. The rest of the team can live on the about page, which must also be readable on this same phone. Do not design a team grid that only works when it is a desktop mural.

Abstract trust lines are even weaker on a phone because they occupy the only lines you had. "Bank-grade security" as the headline has spent the first screen. Replace it before you debate font weight.

## Starting an account on a small screen

If the path is an application, the mobile form is part of the site, not a different product you hope they will finish on a laptop. Ask for the minimum on the first step. Email, entity name, country. Say why you need anything that feels sensitive, in the label, not in a tooltip that is hard to open with a thumb.

Show errors next to the field, in text, when the step fails. Do not clear the form. Do not rely on a red border alone. A buyer on a bus will not infer which field broke. Keep the keyboard from covering the field they are fixing. These are ordinary engineering tasks, and they are the difference between an account start and an abandoned one.

If the path is a sales call, the mobile page should book it or collect a short note. Ten fields on a phone is how you lose the person the homepage just convinced. Name, work email, country, and the job in one sentence are enough to route them. Ask for volume and documents after a person has replied.

Tell them what happens next on the same screen as the button. "You will get a time by email" or "The application takes about ten minutes and asks for a government ID" prevents a nasty surprise. Do not promise a specific response time you have not staffed. Promise the true one.

## Speed and stability are part of the trust

web.dev describes Core Web Vitals as three field measures of experience. Largest Contentful Paint, the loading of the main content, should occur within 2.5 seconds for a good result. Interaction to Next Paint, the responsiveness of a tap, should be 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift, the visual stability of the page, should stay at 0.1 or less. The recommendation is to judge the 75th percentile of visits, split by mobile and desktop.

On this page, LCP is usually the product image or the headline. Ship an image that is the right size for the phone, not a desktop photograph scaled down by the browser. INP is the tap on the account button, including whatever script you attached to it. CLS is the button jumping when a font, a banner, or a chat widget arrives late. A moving button on a money page feels like carelessness. Buyers notice carelessness.

Hanabi builds marketing sites in Next.js on Vercel, with the front end in React, TypeScript, and Tailwind. The stack is not the point. The point is that the phone visit is designed and measured, not hoped for after the desktop is signed off. Motion, if you use it, should not be what pushes the product image past the LCP budget, and it should switch off for people who ask for reduced motion.

Test on a mid-range phone over an ordinary connection, not only on the laptop you designed with. The 75th percentile is not your office wifi. If the product image is the LCP element, treat its weight as a design decision. A tighter crop is often the faster, clearer picture.

## What to drop when the desktop was designed first

If you already have a wide page, edit it down instead of shrinking it.

- Cut the second headline. Keep the sentence that says who it is for.
- Replace the device mock with the interface itself.
- Move logo rows below the first action, or delete them if they have no sentence.
- Collapse secondary calls into text links.
- Remove autoplay video above the product.
- Make the header the wordmark plus the action, with the rest in a short menu.

Then read the page in a mobile browser, not a responsive preview alone. Previews lie about the browser chrome, the font, and the sticky banner your consent tool will add. Those pixels are part of the first screen whether or not they were in the Figma frame.

Check landscape only far enough to see that the button is still reachable. Do not maintain a separate storyboard for it. A buyer turning the phone should not lose the product or the path. That is the whole requirement.

[Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) include this kind of marketing site: a phone-first first screen, a fast build, and a path that still makes sense when the window is narrow.

## Review the visit the way it happens

Give the phone to someone who is not on the project. Ask them to say what the product is, who stands behind it, and what they would tap. Watch their thumb. If they scroll before they can answer, the order is wrong. If they tap and the page jumps, the stability is wrong. If they pinch the screenshot, the proof is too small.

Do the same with the account start or the sales form. Count fields. Count errors you forced on purpose. A good mobile visit is not a miniature desktop. It is the decision, in a column, with a target the thumb can hit.

Once they are ready to reach you, the contact path has to be as clear as the first screen. [A contact path for a fintech product](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-fintech-product) is about what happens after they tap, how fast, and what they should have ready so the form stays short.
